chunks: Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Shammun, from Abdullah ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Misma' ibn Abd al-Malik, from Abu Abdillah عليه السلام, who said:

Amir al-Mu'minin عليه السلام said: ‘The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم ruled that for the ma'mumah there is one-third of the diyah, for the munaqqilah fifteen camels, for the mudihah five camels, for the damiyah one camel, for the badi'ah two camels, and he ruled for the mutalahimah three camels, and he ruled for the simhaq four camels.’

key_terms.الدَّامِيَةِ: a bleeding wound, for which one camel is due
key_terms.الدِّيَةِ: financial compensation due for bodily injury or homicide
key_terms.السِّمْحَاقِ: a wound reaching the thin membrane over the bone, for which four camels are due
key_terms.الْبَاضِعَةِ: a wound that cuts into flesh, for which two camels are due
key_terms.الْمَأْمُومَةِ: a head wound reaching the membrane surrounding the brain, carrying one-third of the full diyah
key_terms.الْمُنَقِّلَةِ: an injury that displaces or breaks bone, for which fifteen camels are due
key_terms.الْمُوضِحَةِ: a wound exposing the bone, for which five camels are due

ai.seo_question: What are the diyah amounts for different kinds of head wounds in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith records a legal ruling transmitted from Amir al-Mu'minin عليه السلام regarding fixed compensation amounts for different categories of head wounds. It reflects the Prophetic sunnah (prophetic tradition) in specifying graded diyah according to the severity of the injury, forming part of the jurisprudence of bodily injury and judicial rulings.
